text:
# The Later Cloud <note>original: Uttara-megha</note>

Of the women with parted hair <term>sīmantinīnām</term> <gloss>married women or wives</gloss>. The <term>Amarakośa</term> <gloss>a famous Sanskrit lexicon</gloss> states: "A woman, a wife with parted hair, a bride." <insert>Brought by a friend</insert> Having been received through a friend or from the mouth of a friend. The word "friend" is used here to remove any fear or suspicion of deception. The news of the beloved <term>kāntodantaḥ</term> means the report or tidings of the husband. The <term>Amarakośa</term> says: "News, movement, account, and tidings are synonyms." This news is "slightly less than a reunion," meaning it brings joy almost equal to the actual contact or physical presence of the beloved.

Now he delivers the message:

O long-lived one, both by my request and to do a service to yourself, speak thus to her: "Your companion, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri, being alive, asks after your welfare, O frail one, though separated from you. For this indeed is the first thing to be asked of living beings whose calamities are easily come by." <note>Verse 41</note>

To her: O long-lived one! <note>The suffix "matup" is used here as praise, implying one whose life is praiseworthy due to helping others.</note> By my <insert>request</insert>, a word of entreaty, and for the sake of doing a service to yourself. This means to make oneself fulfilled by helping others. Although the self is the object of the act of helping, the use of the genitive case "to yourself" <note>original: ātmanaḥ</note> is not incorrect, as it expresses a general relationship. As Bharavi <note>a classical poet</note> says: "That fortune is useful by which one helps others." Likewise, Shriharsha: "To help the virtuous, to see Fortune, to go through the sky." Therefore, the statement of the commentator Natha—that because the second case is seen in some places, it must be so everywhere—is a statement without authority.

To that beloved woman, you should speak in this way. He explains what should be said: "O frail one, your companion and husband, staying in the hermitages of Ramagiri <note>identified as Chitrakuta</note>, is not dead." He gives the reason for this mention: "Being separated and suffering, he asks after your welfare." <note>The verb "to ask" takes two objects according to grammatical rules.</note> For indeed, for living beings whose misfortunes occur without effort, this very inquiry into welfare is the first thing that must necessarily be asked. <note>The suffix "nyat" is used here to denote necessity.</note>

With his body against your body, the very thin with the thin, the fevered with the intensely fevered, the tear-shedding with the tear-filled, the longing with the unceasingly longing... <note>Fragment of Verse 42</note>

<summary>This page contains a commentary on Verse 41 of the Meghaduta, explaining the Yaksha's request to the Cloud to deliver a message of safety and welfare to his wife. It provides grammatical justifications and lexical definitions for the terms used in the poem.</summary>
